Question 1
?

Find the particular solution to the differential equation below that satisfies the condition y(1)=1.

2x+dydx=x2+4x.

a
y=x3+x2−1
b
y=x3+2x2−2
c
y=x33−x2+53
d
y=x33+2x2−43
e
y=x33+x2−13
Submit

decision.explanation: Rearranging gives dy/dx=x^2+2x. Integrating yields y=x^3/3+x^2+C. Since y(1)=1, 1=1/3+1+C, so C=-1/3. Thus option e is correct.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Find the particular solution to the differential equation below that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1.$

$$
2x+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}+4x.
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}+2x.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}+2x)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+2\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $y=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+{x}^{2}+C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $y(1)=1$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+{x}^{2}+C \\ 1 & =\frac{{1}^{3}}{3}+{1}^{2}+C \\ 1 & =\frac{4}{3}+C \\ C & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
y=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Question 1
?

Find the particular solution to the differential equation below that satisfies the condition y(1)=1.

2x+dydx=x2+4x.

a
y=x3+x2−1
b
y=x3+2x2−2
c
y=x33−x2+53
d
y=x33+2x2−43
e
y=x33+x2−13
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we rearrange the equation to give

dydx=x2+2x.

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to x, and get

∫dydxdx=∫(x2+2x)dxy=x33+2⋅x22+C=x33+x2+C.

So our general solution is y=x33+x2+C. To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition y(1)=1 into our solution and obtain a value for C, as follows:

y=x33+x2+C1=133+12+C1=43+CC=−13.

Therefore, our particular solution is y=x33+x2−13.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Solution of a Differential Equation With a Given Condition
content.problem:
Find the particular solution to the differential equation below that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1.$

$$
2x+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}+4x.
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}+2x.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}+2x)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+2\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $y=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+{x}^{2}+C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $y(1)=1$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+{x}^{2}+C \\ 1 & =\frac{{1}^{3}}{3}+{1}^{2}+C \\ 1 & =\frac{4}{3}+C \\ C & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
y=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Question 3
?

Solve the differential equation d2ydx2−2x=cos⁡x.

a
y=2xln2⁡2−sin⁡x+Cx+D
b
y=2xln⁡2−cos⁡x+Cx+D
c
y=2xln⁡2+cos⁡x+Cx+D
d
y=2xln2⁡2−cos⁡x+Cx+D
e
y=2xln2⁡2+sin⁡x+Cx+D
Submit

decision.explanation: Rearrange to y''=2^x+cos(x). Integrating twice gives y'=2^x/ln(2)+sin(x)+C and y=2^x/(ln(2))^2-cos(x)+Cx+D, which matches option d.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{2}^{x}.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{2}^{x})\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x+\int {2}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{{2}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{{2}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C)\text{d}x \\ y & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {2}^{x}\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\frac{{2}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2})+Cx+D \\  & =\frac{{2}^{x}}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get ∫d2ydx2dx=∫(cos⁡x+2x)dxdydx=∫cos⁡xdx+∫2xdx=sin⁡x+2xln⁡2+C.

Integrating a second time, we get ∫dydxdx=∫(sin⁡x+2xln⁡2+C)dxy=∫sin⁡xdx+1ln⁡2∫2xdx+C∫dx=−cos⁡x+1ln⁡2(2xln⁡2)+Cx+D=2xln2⁡2−cos⁡x+Cx+D.

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains two arbitrary constants, C and D.

content.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{2}^{x}.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{2}^{x})\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x+\int {2}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{{2}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{{2}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C)\text{d}x \\ y & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {2}^{x}\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\frac{{2}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2})+Cx+D \\  & =\frac{{2}^{x}}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

after.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{8}{(x-3)^{2}}.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {y}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{8}{(x-3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ y & =8\int \frac{1}{(x-3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =8(-\frac{1}{x-3})+C \\  & =-\frac{8}{x-3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $y=-\frac{8}{x-3}+C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $y(4)=1$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-\frac{8}{4-3}+C \\ 1 & =-8+C \\ C & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
y=-\frac{8}{x-3}+9.
$$
